'''Michael S. Turner''' (born July 29, 1949)<ref name="AIP">{{cite web |title=Turner, Michael Stanley |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11610020.html |website=American Institute of Physics |access-date=18 October 2022 |archive-date=October 18, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221018220305/https://history.aip.org/phn/11610020.html |url-status=live }}</ref> is an American theoretical [[Physical cosmology|cosmologist]] who coined the term ''[[dark energy]]'' in 1998.<ref name="Stromlo">{{cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Michael S. |title=The Third Stromlo Symposium, the galactic halo : proceedings of a symposium held at Australian Academy of Science, Canberra, Australia, 17-21 August, 1998 |date=1999 |publisher=Astronomical Society of the Pacific |location=San Francisco, Calif. |isbn=1-886733-86-4 |volume=165 |page=431 |url=http://www.aspbooks.org/a/volumes/article_details/?paper_id=17135 |editor-last1=Gibson |editor-first1=Brad K. |editor-last2=Axelrod |editor-first2=Rim S. |editor-last3=Putman |editor-first3=Mary E. |access-date=18 October 2022 |archive-date=October 18, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221018202905/http://www.aspbooks.org/a/volumes/article_details/?paper_id=17135 |url-status=live }}</ref>
He is the Rauner Distinguished Service Professor Emeritus of Physics at the [[University of Chicago]],<ref name="Lerner">{{cite news |last1=Lerner |first1=Louise |title=UChicago scientists to help lay out vision for future of particle physics {{!}} University of Chicago News |url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/uchicago-scientists-help-lay-out-vision-future-particle-physics |access-date=18 October 2022 |work=UChicago News |date=October 3, 2022 |language=en}}</ref> having previously served as the Bruce V. & Diana M. Rauner Distinguished Service Professor,<ref name="uchicago"/> and as the assistant director for Mathematical and Physical Sciences for the US [[National Science Foundation]].<ref name="AIP"/>

Turner's book ''The Early Universe'', co-written with fellow Chicago cosmologist [[Edward Kolb]], is a standard text on the subject.<ref name="Egan">{{cite journal |last1=Egan |first1=Chas A. |last2=Charles H. |first2=Lineweaver |title=A Larger Estimate of the Entropy of the Universe |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=2010 |volume=710 |issue=2 |pages=1825–1834 |doi=10.1088/0004-637x/710/2/1825 |arxiv=0909.3983 |bibcode=2010ApJ...710.1825E |s2cid=1274173 |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0004-637X/710/2/1825 |access-date=18 October 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Press |first1=W. H. |title=The Early Universe. Edward W. Kolb and Michael S. Turner. Addison-Wesley, Redwood City, CA, 1990. xxii, 547 pp., illus. $48.50. Frontiers in Physics, 69 |journal=Science |date=17 August 1990 |volume=249 |issue=4970 |pages=808–809 |doi=10.1126/science.249.4970.808-a |pmid=17756792 |language=en |issn=0036-8075}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Kolb |first1=Edward W. |last2=Turner |first2=Michael S. |title=The early universe |date=1990 |publisher=Addison-Wesley Publishing Company, Inc. |location=Reading, MA |isbn= }}</ref> 
The 2003 National Academy study, ''Connecting quarks with the cosmos: eleven science questions for the new century'', which Turner chaired, identified opportunities at the intersection of astronomy and physics and has helped shape science investment in the US in this area.<ref>{{cite book |title=Connecting Quarks with the Cosmos: Eleven Science Questions for the New Century |date=12 March 2003 |publisher=National Academies Press |location=Washington, D.C. |isbn=0-309-07406-1 |author=Committee on the Physics of the Universe, Board on Physics and Astronomy, Division on Engineering and Physical Sciences, National Research Council of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine |doi=10.17226/10079 |url= https://doi.org/10.17226/10079}}</ref> 
In 2022, Turner was appointed as a co-leader, with [[Maria Spiropulu]], of a National Academies of Science, Engineering and Medicine study, leading a committee of 17 physicists world-wide to consider the strategic vision of research in elementary particle physics.<ref name="Lerner"/>

==Education==
Turner received a [[B.S.]] in physics from the [[California Institute of Technology]] in 1971 and earned a PhD in physics from [[Stanford University]] in 1978.<ref name="Chandra">{{cite web |title=Chandra Press Room :: CXC Biographies :: Michael S. Turner |url=https://chandra.harvard.edu/press/bios/turner_bio.html |website=Chandra X-ray Observatory |access-date=18 October 2022}}</ref>

==Career==
Turner became an instructor in physics at Stanford University in 1978 and was a fellow at the [[Enrico Fermi Institute]] from 1978 to 1980. He was a visiting professor at the Institute for Theoretical Physics at the University of California, Santa Barbara, from 1981 to 1982 and became a scientist at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Batavia, Ill, in 1983.<ref name="AIP"/>

Turner joined the faculty of the [[University of Chicago]] as an assistant professor of astronomy and astrophysics in 1980, rising to associate professor and then full professor as of 1985. He served as chair of the department from 1997 to 2003 and was named the Bruce V. and Diana M. Rauner Distinguished Service Professor of Astronomy and Astrophysics in 1998.<ref name="AIP"/>  He held a joint appointment as one of the founding members of the NASA/Fermilab Theoretical Astrophysics Group at the NASA [[Fermilab]] Astrophysics Center (NFAC).<ref name="Grim"/><ref name="Turner"/>

In addition, Turner served as the president of the [[Aspen Center for Physics]] from 1989 to 1993 and as the assistant director of the National Science Foundation for Mathematical and Physical Sciences from 2003 to 2006.<ref name="AIP"/> He has served on committees for the Department of Energy, NASA, NSF, the American Physical Society, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the National Academy of Sciences.<ref name="Chandra"/> Turner was president of the [[American Physical Society]] in 2013.<ref name="AIP"/>

From 2010 to 2019, Turner served as director of the Kavli Institute for Cosmological Physics at the University of Chicago. He was succeeded as director by [[Edward Kolb]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Edward 'Rocky' Kolb to direct Kavli Institute for Cosmological Physics {{!}} University of Chicago News |url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/edward-rocky-kolb-direct-kavli-institute-cosmological-physics |access-date=18 October 2022 |work=UChicago News |date=Feb 26, 2019 |language=en |archive-date=October 18, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221018225935/https://news.uchicago.edu/story/edward-rocky-kolb-direct-kavli-institute-cosmological-physics |url-status=live }}</ref>
By 2020, Turner was the Rauner Distinguished Service Professor Emeritus of Physics at UChicago.<ref>{{cite news |title=Two $5 million gifts to support Kavli Institute for Cosmological Physics {{!}} University of Chicago News |url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/two-5-million-gifts-support-kavli-institute-cosmological-physics |access-date=18 October 2022 |work=UChicago News |date=September 30, 2020 |language=en |archive-date=October 18, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221018225933/https://news.uchicago.edu/story/two-5-million-gifts-support-kavli-institute-cosmological-physics |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Research==
With [[Edward Kolb]], Turner helped establish the interdisciplinary field of particle astrophysics, combining cosmology and elementary particle physics to understand the origin and evolution of the Universe.<ref name="Grim">{{cite news |last1=Grim |first1=Kathryn |title=Fermilab physicists honored for uniting physics and cosmology |url=https://www.fnal.gov/pub/today/archive/archive_2010/today10-02-16_readmore.html |access-date=18 October 2022 |work=Fermilab Today |date=2010 |archive-date=June 25, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240625105405/https://www.fnal.gov/pub/today/archive/archive_2010/today10-02-16_readmore.html |url-status=live }}</ref>  His research focuses on the earliest moments of creation, and he has made contributions to inflationary cosmology, particle dark matter and structure formation, the theory of big bang nucleosynthesis, and the nature of dark energy.<ref name="uchicago">{{cite web |title=Michael S. Turner |url=https://astro.uchicago.edu/people/michael-s-turner.php |website=The Department of Astronomy and Astrophysics |access-date=18 October 2022 |archive-date=September 29, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220929115204/https://astro.uchicago.edu/people/michael-s-turner.php |url-status=live }}</ref>  His work in [[precision cosmology]] combines theoretical work with measurement to better understand and test theories and models using cosmological data.<ref name="NAS">{{cite web |title=Michael S. Turner |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/michael-s-turner-glbwlc/ |website=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=18 October 2022}}</ref><ref name="Turner">{{cite journal |last1=Turner |first1=Michael S. |title=The Road to Precision Cosmology |journal=Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science |date=26 September 2022 |volume=72 |issue=1 |pages=1–35 |doi=10.1146/annurev-nucl-111119-041046 |arxiv=2201.04741 |bibcode=2022ARNPS..72....1T |s2cid=245906450 |language=en |issn=0163-8998|doi-access=free }}</ref>
